topic: The Pi Collision Puzzle: Calculating Pi through Physics
target_audience: High school students and university undergraduates with basic physics and geometry knowledge

outline.topic: The Pi Collision Puzzle: Calculating Pi through Physics
outline.target_audience: High school students and university undergraduates with basic physics and geometry knowledge

sections.title: Introduction: The Impossible Connection
sections.content: Introduce a simple physical scenario: a wall, a small block (mass m), and a large block (mass M). The large block slides toward the small block, which is sitting between the wall and the large block. Ask the audience: 'How many times will these objects collide?'
sections.example: Imagine a tiny mouse (mass m) sitting between a wall and a giant elephant (mass M) riding a skateboard. Every time the elephant hits the mouse, or the mouse hits the wall, we count it as one 'clack'.

sections.title: Setting the Rules: Elastic Collisions
sections.content: Define the physical constraints. 1. No friction. 2. Perfectly elastic collisions (kinetic energy and momentum are conserved). 3. The wall is immovable. Introduce the variables for velocity and mass.
sections.example: Visualize the blocks as frictionless pucks on an air-hockey table. Use color-coded vectors (arrows) to show the velocity of each block after every 'clack'.

sections.title: The Pattern Emerges: Counting the Clacks
sections.content: Demonstrate the results for different mass ratios. When M = m, there are 3 collisions. When M = 100m, there are 31 collisions. When M = 10,000m, there are 314 collisions. Highlight the appearing digits of Pi.
sections.example: Show a digital counter above the blocks. Ratio 1:1 -> '3'. Ratio 100:1 -> '31'. Ratio 1,000,000:1 -> '3141'. The audience should see the digits of Pi appearing as M increases by powers of 100.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Conservation Laws as Geometry
sections.content: Explain that conservation of energy (1/2 Mv² + 1/2 mu² = E) represents an ellipse in a velocity-space graph (v, u). By rescaling the x-axis by sqrt(M), the ellipse transforms into a perfect circle.
sections.example: An animation morphing a stretched-out oval (ellipse) into a perfect circle by scaling the 'Big Block Velocity' axis. This circle represents all possible states of the system.

sections.title: The Geometric Insight: The Bouncing Beam
sections.content: Map each collision to a point on the circle. A block-block collision follows momentum conservation, which looks like a reflection across a specific line. A wall collision (changing direction of the small block) is a reflection across the u-axis.
sections.example: Show a laser beam bouncing inside a circular mirror. Each time the beam hits the edge of the circle, it represents one collision in the real world. The total number of collisions is the number of 'hits' before the beam exits the arc.

sections.title: The Grand Conclusion: Why Pi?
sections.content: Explain that as the mass ratio M/m becomes very large, the angle of each 'bounce' on the circle becomes very small. The total number of collisions is the total arc length covered divided by the step size, which leads directly to the formula involving Pi.
sections.example: Overlay a circle of radius 1 onto the block simulation. Show that the total number of steps is equal to the circumference (2π) divided by the tiny angle θ, which is approximately the square root of the mass ratio.

sections.title: Summary and Takeaway
sections.content: Recap how a purely kinetic counting puzzle reveals a fundamental mathematical constant. Emphasize that Pi isn't just about circles, but about the deep symmetry in conservation laws.
sections.example: A final side-by-side shot: the blocks finishing their collisions on one side, and the digits of Pi (3.1415...) glowing on the other, linked by a circular arc.

storyboard.title: Introduction: The Impossible Connection
lecture_lines: Imagine a small block between a wall and large block.
The large block slides toward the small one.
How many collisions will occur in this setup?
animations: A white wall (#FFFFFF), a small green block (#52C41A), and a large blue block (#1890FF) appear on a black background.
The large blue block (#1890FF) begins sliding left toward the stationary small green block (#52C41A).
Text 'How many collisions will occur?' appears in white (#FFFFFF) above the blocks.

storyboard.title: Setting the Rules: Elastic Collisions
lecture_lines: We assume no friction and perfectly elastic collisions.
Momentum and kinetic energy are fully conserved.
The wall is immovable, reflecting the small block.
animations: The blocks flash briefly to indicate a frictionless surface.
Velocity vectors appear as blue (#1890FF) and green (#52C41A) arrows on the blocks.
The wall is highlighted as a fixed white (#FFFFFF) vertical line on the left.

storyboard.title: The Pattern Emerges: Counting the Clacks
lecture_lines: Let's vary the mass of the large block.
With equal masses, we count exactly three collisions.
Increase the mass ratio to one hundred to one.
Now we count thirty-one collisions.
The digits of Pi begin to emerge clearly.
animations: Set M = m. Blocks collide 3 times; a red counter (#FF4D4F) shows '3'.
Set M = 100m. 31 collisions occur; the red counter (#FF4D4F) updates to '31'.
Set M = 10,000m. 314 collisions occur; the red counter (#FF4D4F) updates to '314'.
Set M = 1,000,000m. 3141 collisions occur; the red counter (#FF4D4F) updates to '3141'.
The digits 3, 1, 4, 1 in the counter flash in red (#FF4D4F) to highlight the pattern.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Conservation Laws as Geometry
lecture_lines: Conservation of energy creates an elliptical state space.
Rescaling the velocity axes transforms this into a circle.
Every state of the system lies on this circle.
Collisions move the system's state along the circle.
Physics is now transformed into a geometric problem.
animations: Display the energy conservation equation 1/2 Mv² + 1/2 mu² = E in white (#FFFFFF).
A yellow (#FADB14) ellipse is plotted on a graph with v and u axes.
The v-axis scales by sqrt(M), transforming the yellow ellipse into a perfect circle.

storyboard.title: The Geometric Insight: The Bouncing Beam
lecture_lines: Each collision acts like a reflection within the circle.
Wall hits and block hits create distinct bounce patterns.
The process resembles a beam of light bouncing inside.
animations: Place a red point (#FF4D4F) on the yellow circle boundary to represent the initial state.
A white line (#FFFFFF) reflects across a diameter to represent a block-block collision.
A white line (#FFFFFF) reflects vertically to represent a wall collision.
A zigzag beam (#FFFFFF) begins bouncing around the inside of the yellow circle.
Each point where the beam hits the circle boundary flashes in red (#FF4D4F).

storyboard.title: The Grand Conclusion: Why Pi?
lecture_lines: Large mass ratios result in very small bounce angles.
Each collision covers a tiny arc of the circle.
Total collisions equal the total arc divided by step.
This ratio directly relates to the circle's circumference.
Pi appears because we are traversing a geometric circle.
animations: Zoom in on a small section of the yellow circle to show a tiny arc.
Label the angle between collision points as theta, colored red (#FF4D4F).
Show the relation theta ≈ sqrt(m/M) in white text (#FFFFFF).
The total number of collisions N is shown as pi divided by theta.
The symbol Pi (#FF4D4F) grows and glows to emphasize the connection.

storyboard.title: Summary and Takeaway
lecture_lines: We calculated Pi using only blocks and collisions.
Conservation laws reveal deep, hidden geometric symmetries.
Mathematics and physics are fundamentally and beautifully linked.
animations: The blocks perform their final clacks on the left side of the screen.
The digits 3.1415... glow in red (#FF4D4F) on the right side.
A yellow (#FADB14) circular arc connects the blocks to the digits of Pi.
